newsitem.title: ZAMBIA: Zambian president races ahead in boycotted polls.
newsitem.headline: Zambian president races ahead in boycotted polls.

text.p: Zambian President Frederick Chiluba raced ahead as results came in on Tuesday from presidential elections which his main rival, former president Kenneth Kaunda, was forbidden from contending.
"Results so far countrywide show President Chiluba has scooped votes so far," state radio said in the morning.

In most places Chiluba, who ousted Kaunda in 1991 in the country's first free elections in decades, won 10 times as many votes as any of his four remaining rivals who analysts had seen as political minnows all along.
Chiluba's Movement for Multi-party Democracy (MMD), which won 125 out of 150 seats last time round, looked set to retain its domination in the simultaneous parliamentary elections.
Eleven parties stood on Monday but MMD won nearly all the first few seats to be declared.

Regional leaders from one main contending opposition party, the Zambian Democratic Congress, stormed the television station in one provincial town, saying the election had been rigged. They were ejected by paramilitary police, the radio said.

Kaunda's United National Independence Party (UNIP) walked out of parliament in protest at a constitutional amendment in May which they and Western donors say was introduced to bar the only man who might have given Chiluba, 53, a real fight.
The new law said that only people whose parents were born in Zambia could stand for president.
Kaunda, who ruled the country for 27 years from independence from Britain in 1964, has Malawian parents.
UNIP were closely watching the size of voter turnout in Monday's polls to see how successful their call for a mass boycott had been.
No final figures were ready but both camps claimed success.
The pro-opposition Post newspaper said its survey showed a 40 percent turnout of people who collected their voter cards.

But only a quarter of the 4.6 million eligible voters were given polling cards, due to a flawed computer registration system. Thousands of people were given wrong polling cards and many others obtained no cards at all.
The pro-government press said UNIP had failed in its boycott and failed to incite violence.
"The prophets of doom can eat their hearts out -- Zambia is still intact," the Times of Zambia wrote.
"The massive turnout of voters and almost serene atmosphere countrywide was irrefutable evidence that UNIP's election boycott was a total flop."
"It's a blunder UNIP, and particularly Dr Kaunda, will live to regret."

By calling the boycott Kaunda has put his party's future on the line. He says he expects Chiluba's government to last only six months before fresh and fairer elections are called but many political analysts said they doubted that.
Casting his vote, Chiluba said he would reopen dialogue with the opposition but did not say if that meant UNIP too.
He also said he had nothing to fear from a planned court appeal by opponents who, hoping to beat him with his own stick, questioned how Zambian the president's own parents were.
Western donors froze vital aid that helps keep the copper-rich but debt-ridden southern African country afloat to protest at the constitutional amendment.

They now face a hard choice: watch the freeze scupper Chiluba's attempts to turn the ravaged economy around through World Bank-approved privatisation and austerity measures, or turn a blind eye to the poll's shortcomings and resume aid.
